provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.6% in February 20261, the highest level in the province since early 2021, as the labour market absorbed the combined effects of U.S. tariff uncertainty on trade-exposed manufacturing and a slowdown in residential construction activity. Toronto CMA housing starts declined 28% year-over-year in February2, reflecting elevated borrowing costs and reduced buyer qualification volumes. The project database tracks 652 Ontario projects, of which 220 are in rate-sensitive sectors3 — residential, commercial, and mixed-use developments whose timelines are directly linked to financing conditions and mortgage rate movements.

The Ontario 2026 Budget, released March 26, introduced a $210 billion 10-year capital plan — the largest in provincial history — with $37 billion allocated for fiscal year 2026-27.4 Of that total, $63 billion is directed to transit expansion (Ontario Line, Yonge North Subway Extension, Scarborough Subway Extension, Hamilton LRT), $64 billion to health infrastructure covering 50+ hospital projects and approximately 3,000 new beds, and $31 billion to highways including Highway 413 (now under construction) and the Bradford Bypass.56 The budget projects a $13.8 billion deficit for 2026-27, with total spending of $244.2 billion against revenues of $231.9 billion.4

A temporary HST rebate on new homes is estimated to generate 8,000 housing starts and provide $2.2 billion in joint tax relief.7 The Eglinton Crosstown LRT opened in February 2026, delivering 19 km of rapid transit including 10 km underground.8 The small business corporate income tax rate was reduced from 3.2% to 2.2%, with estimated relief of $1.1 billion to over 375,000 small businesses over three years.4 A $4 billion Protect Ontario Account Investment Fund targets AI, defence, advanced manufacturing, and life sciences.9 The database tracks 150 projects in employment-sensitive sectors (healthcare, education, manufacturing, government) and 205 infrastructure projects in Ontario.3

provinces.labourDeepDive: Labour Market: Ontario shed jobs in February as unemployment rose to 7.6% from 7.3% the prior month, a 0.3 percentage point increase.1 The province tracks 150 projects in employment-sensitive sectors including healthcare, education, manufacturing, and government.3 The small business corporate income tax reduction from 3.2% to 2.2% is estimated to provide $1.1 billion in relief to over 375,000 small businesses over three years, with potential implications for small-firm hiring decisions.4
provinces.consumerPulse: Ontario's CPI index rose to 173.0 in February 2026 from 172.0 the prior month.1 The temporary HST rebate on new homes valued up to $1 million — part of an $8.8 billion cost-matched federal-provincial housing agreement — covers municipalities representing approximately 80% of Ontario's population, with municipal development charges reduced by up to 50%.7 The budget deficit of $13.8 billion for 2026-27 represents the gap between $244.2 billion in spending and $231.9 billion in revenues.4

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec recorded the largest provincial employment decline in February 2026, shedding 57,000 positions (-1.2%), which pushed the unemployment rate up 0.7 percentage points to 5.9%.1 This represents the steepest single-month job loss in Quebec since the pandemic period. The project database tracks 212 projects in employment-sensitive sectors across the province, including manufacturing, healthcare, and government services.2

The Quebec Budget 2026-27, tabled with a projected $8.6 billion deficit within a $170.8 billion budget, adds $5 billion over six years to infrastructure spending, bringing the 10-year Quebec Infrastructure Plan (QIP) to $167 billion.3 Of the QIP total, $105.8 billion (71%) is designated for asset maintenance, with $3.6 billion for hospitals, $1.2 billion for public transit, and $631 million for higher education.4 An additional $1.7 billion over five years targets economic transformation, including $480 million for critical and strategic minerals.3 The deficit is projected to decline to $1.5 billion by 2028-29.3

Montreal CMA housing starts rose 18% year-over-year in February 20265, contrasting with the labour market contraction. The database contains 132 rate-sensitive Quebec projects in the residential and commercial pipeline.2 Building permits issued in January 2026 totalled $25.87 billion for residential and $10.27 billion for non-residential categories.6 The REM A3 branch to the West Island is scheduled to open in Q2 2026, and the Quebec City Tramway is under active construction on a 5 km span with operations targeted for 2033.7 The database tracks 493 Quebec projects in total.2

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta's unemployment rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 6.3% in February 20261, as the province's energy sector continued to operate against WTI crude oil at US$102.18/bbl.2 The Alberta Budget 2026, tabled by Finance Minister Nate Horner, projects a $9.4 billion deficit for 2026-27 — more than double the 2025-26 shortfall — driven by a projected $8.8 billion decline in non-renewable resource revenue from 2024-25 levels.3 The budget forecasts WTI at US$60/bbl, compared to a private-sector average of US$58/bbl, and projects oil sands royalties of $9.7 billion and conventional oil royalties of $2.1 billion.3

The three-year capital plan totals $28.3 billion, an increase of $2.2 billion over the previous budget, with $7.1 billion for municipal infrastructure and $4.9 billion for health capital.3 The Trans Mountain pipeline is operating at or near full capacity, with a 10% throughput increase achieved through drag-reducing agents (DRA).4 The Dow Fort Saskatchewan petrochemical complex — a $11.6 billion facility — remains under construction with completion expected by 2029.5 Alberta has also authorized $900 million in borrowing authority for a potential new pipeline to the northern BC coast.6

The project database tracks 727 Alberta projects in total, with 209 energy-sector projects and 243 employment-sensitive projects.7 Alberta's CPI index rose to 202.1 from 201.7 the prior month.1 Two proposed Beacon AI data centre hubs — one in Rocky View County ($100 billion) and one in Leduc County ($100 billion) — are listed in the Alberta Major Projects inventory, representing the scale of AI infrastructure proposals currently in the provincial pipeline.8

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.analysis:
British Columbia's unemployment rate held steady at 6.1% in February 20261, despite employment declining by 20,000 positions over the month, as labour force exits offset the reduction in employment. Vancouver CMA housing starts surged 60% year-over-year in February2, the largest year-over-year increase among major Canadian CMAs, providing a counterpoint to the provincial government's decision to reallocate $1.4 billion from housing programs over three years and close the Community Housing Fund indefinitely.3 The database contains 138 rate-sensitive projects in BC's residential and commercial pipeline.4

BC Budget 2026 projects a $13.3 billion deficit — the largest in provincial history — with nearly $38 billion in capital projects across the fiscal plan.3 Capital commitments include 17 major hospital projects, the Broadway Subway, and the Surrey Langley SkyTrain extension.3 GDP growth is forecast at 1.3% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027 (TD Economics).5 The province also records the highest-ever forecast for nonresidential construction spending in 2026.3

LNG Canada Phase 1 ($47.9 billion) at Kitimat is under construction, while Phase 2 — which would double capacity from 14 Mt/y to 28 Mt/y — is in proposed status at an estimated $25 billion.6 The Kitimat Clean Oil Refinery ($22 billion), proposed to process 400,000 bbl/d of Alberta oil sands bitumen, is under review.7 The database tracks 660 BC projects in total, with 158 energy-sector projects.4 The BC government announced two new rental buildings in West Vancouver expanding housing options for workers and families with middle incomes.8

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.6% in February 20261, as employment declined by 5,500 positions over the month. Building construction investment in the province increased 25.6% year-over-year in January 2026, one of the highest growth rates nationally.2 The project database tracks 213 Saskatchewan projects and 34 energy-sector and mining projects.3

Saskatchewan Budget 2026 projects an $819 million deficit — the largest budgeted shortfall in 15 years outside the COVID period — with $1.8 billion in core government infrastructure spending and a total capital investment plan of $4.3 billion including Crown corporation allocations.4 Potash royalties are projected at $940.9 million for 2026-27, exceeding oil sector earnings at $721 million, marking a shift in the province's resource revenue composition.4

BHP's Jansen potash mine — a $14 billion investment with potential capacity of 8.5 Mt/y — is expected to begin production in late 2026.5 The K+S Bethune mine expansion, estimated at up to $3 billion, would double potash production from 2 Mt to 4 Mt annually.5 By end of 2026, Saskatchewan is expected to have commercial production of six critical minerals: potash, uranium, helium, copper, zinc, and lithium.4 Bell Canada announced a $1.7 billion AI data centre in Saskatchewan, described as the largest in Canada, projecting $12 billion in economic value and over 1,630 jobs.6

provinces.consumerPulse: Saskatchewan's CPI index rose to 130.0 from 129.6 the prior month.1 The province's $819 million budgeted deficit reflects revenue pressures from declining oil royalties, partially offset by rising potash royalties at $940.9 million.4

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.analysis:
Manitoba recorded the largest provincial unemployment decline in February 2026, falling 0.6 percentage points to 5.7% from 6.3% the prior month1, despite employment declining by 4,000 positions, as labour force exits exceeded the employment decline. Year-over-year, employment rose 1.8% (+12,900 positions) from January 2025 to January 2026.2 Nominal GDP growth was 4.4% in 2025, with a 3.6% forecast for 2026 (Manitoba Bureau of Statistics).2

Manitoba Budget 2026, tabled March 25, reports a $498 million deficit — down from $1.7 billion in 2025-26 — with a surplus of $8 million projected for 2027-28.3 The budget includes a record $3.8 billion capital investment plan covering roads, hospitals, schools, and community infrastructure, with a five-year capital plan averaging $4.3 billion annually.3 The PST was removed from groceries effective 2026.4 The database tracks 2,058 Manitoba projects and 616 infrastructure projects.5

Winnipeg's North End Water Pollution Control Centre (NEWPCC) — a $3.2 billion upgrade — reached a milestone on March 18 with UV disinfection treatment restored after being shut off for upgrade work.6 The Portage Place redevelopment ($650 million), including a 300,000 sq ft, 12-storey Healthcare Centre of Excellence, is on schedule with demolition of the atrium continuing.7 Nominal exports to the U.S. declined 18% in 2025 across energy, agricultural machinery, and pharmaceuticals categories.4 The Trans-Canada Highway twinning to Ontario is among the infrastructure highlights, alongside health centre construction in 5 communities and $22 million in water infrastructure investments.3

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia's unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 7.1% in February 20261, the highest reading among Atlantic provinces except Newfoundland. The CPI index edged down to 189.5 from 189.6, representing a marginal decline in the price level over the month.1 The project database tracks 339 Nova Scotia projects and 119 energy-sector projects.2

Nova Scotia's Capital Plan 2026-27 is the largest in provincial history at $3.5 billion, with $1.5 billion allocated to the "More, Faster: Action for Health Build" plan.3 Of that healthcare allocation, $1.2 billion is directed to the Halifax Infirmary expansion and Cape Breton Regional Hospital redevelopment.3 An additional $873.8 million targets 5,700 new and replacement long-term care spaces by 2032.3 Budget 2026-27 projects a $1.24 billion deficit, with the debt-to-GDP ratio projected to breach the 40% guardrail by 2027-28.4 Health spending rose 6% to $6.7 billion.4

The Wind West offshore wind project proposes 5 GW of capacity, with Hydro-Quebec issuing a formal request for information to assess feasibility of connecting its grid with Nova Scotia's proposed wind farms.5 Federal defence spending in Nova Scotia includes a $2 billion package, with $1.2 billion allocated to upgrade power and service infrastructure at CFB Halifax Dockyard and Stadacona.6 Public sector headcount reductions are projected to generate $914.3 million in cumulative savings by 2029-30.4

provinces.name: New Brunswick
provinces.analysis:
New Brunswick's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.0% in February 20261, the fourth consecutive monthly increase, as the province's labour market reflects slowing economic momentum. Real GDP growth is estimated at 1.3% in 2025 (Scotiabank), slowing to 1.0% projected for 2026.2 The CPI index fell to 133.3 from 134.1, a decline of 0.8 points over the month — the largest CPI decline among all provinces.1

New Brunswick Budget 2026-27 projects a $1.33 billion deficit, with health spending rising $710 million year-over-year.3 Capital spending is increasing from $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, a $300 million expansion.3 Net debt is projected to rise from $13.9 billion to $19.7 billion by FY2029.3 The database tracks 204 New Brunswick projects, with 45 infrastructure projects and 16 energy-sector projects.4

The nuclear energy sector is a key development area for New Brunswick. NB Power and ARC Clean Technology are advancing the Point Lepreau Small Modular Reactor (ARC-100) proposal, and an NB Power review recommended building a second large nuclear plant adjacent to Point Lepreau.5 Medical isotope production is also being explored at the Point Lepreau site.5 ProEnergy Canada has proposed a $3.5 billion power generation facility in the Tantramar region near Moncton.6 The Saint John Pulp Mill Upgrades ($1.1 billion) are under review at Natural Resources Canada.7

provinces.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's unemployment rate held steady at 9.2% in February 20261, the highest among all provinces, while employment increased by 2,100 positions (+0.8%) — one of only two provinces to record employment gains during the month.2 The simultaneous increase in employment and unchanged unemployment rate indicates that labour force entrants matched the pace of job creation. The CPI index edged up to 166.4 from 166.2.1

The Bay du Nord offshore oil project — estimated at $14 billion in total investment — reached life-of-field agreements on benefits, royalties, and equity with Equinor and BP in March 2026.3 The agreement includes government revenue of up to $6.4 billion from Phase 1, with production capacity of 160,000-175,000 bbl/d and first oil expected in 2031.3 Over the 25-year project life, Bay du Nord is projected to generate 31 million person-hours of work.3 Offshore oil contributes approximately 20% of provincial GDP and 55% of total exports, sustaining approximately 20,000 jobs.4

The project database tracks 1,549 Newfoundland and Labrador projects and 144 energy-sector projects.5 The Grassy Point LNG project ($10 billion) remains in proposed status.6 The White Rose expansion ($3.8 billion West component and $2.3 billion North/South components) is under construction offshore Newfoundland.6 The Kamistiatusset (Kami) iron ore project ($3.9 billion) in Labrador West is under review.6 Net debt is projected at $19.4 billion (44.7% of GDP).4

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island's unemployment rate fell 0.4 percentage points to 7.2% in February 20261, as employment reached an all-time high of 96,200 — the highest level on record for the province.2 Population increased 1.6% to 182,657 (through July 2025), international exports rose 12.8%, and tourism overnight stays increased 4.5%, all contributing to employment demand.2

PEI's capital budget for 2026-27 allocates $486.5 million for the fiscal year and $1.6 billion over five years.3 The five-year plan includes $538 million for healthcare infrastructure, $65.4 million for three new elementary schools, and $100 million for more than 300 new affordable housing units plus $28 million for upgrades and repairs to existing public housing stock.3 The Mental Health Campus project ($131 million) is under construction with completion targeted for 2027-28.4

The current 2025-26 forecast deficit has widened to $367.4 million, a $183.4 million increase from the original budget.2 The spring legislature opened March 25 with budget cuts anticipated. No 2026-27 operating budget has been tabled as of March 31.2 The project database tracks 96 PEI projects, with 20 employment-sensitive projects and 43 rate-sensitive projects.5

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Yukon's unemployment rate stood at 3.6% in January 2026, the lowest among all provinces and territories1, while the labour force participation rate of 74.4% was the highest in Canada.1 These figures indicate the territory's labour market is operating near full capacity. GDP is projected to decline 2.3% in 2025 before a recovery supported by mineral prices.2

Yukon Budget 2026-27 totals $2.46 billion with a projected $81.8 million deficit and a capital budget of $385 million.2 The federal government announced a $40 billion Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment package that includes Yukon forward operating locations, military upgrades, roads, and hydro-power expansion.3 The Whitehorse Power Centres Project proposes two new thermal power centres offering up to 150 megawatts through LNG and diesel, with the south centre targeted for winter 2027 and the north centre for winter 2028.4

The Casino Mine ($3.6 billion), located 150 km northwest of Carmacks, remains in proposed status.5 The Kudz Ze Kayah metals mining project ($489 million) is under IAAC review.5 The Yukon government announced initiatives to improve energy grid reliability, with an estimated $1 billion in grid investment proposed.6 The project database tracks 125 Yukon projects, with 15 employment-sensitive projects and 60 rate-sensitive projects.7

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories' unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.3% in February 20261, as the territory contends with a structural transition in its resource economy. All three producing diamond mines — Diavik (closing 2026), Ekati (2029), and Gahcho Kue (2030) — are scheduled to cease operations by 2030, removing a primary employer and revenue source.2 Employment decreased 3.4% between 2023 and 2024, reflecting the contraction underway.2

NWT Budget 2026-27 totals $2.724 billion with no new taxes introduced.3 The Mining Incentive Program was updated with the $500,000 lifetime cap conditionally removed for corporate projects, while the $1.5 million annual budget was maintained.3 PM Carney announced a $35 billion+ Arctic defence and northern infrastructure plan including $32 billion at Forward Operating Locations in Yellowknife and Inuvik, plus the Mackenzie Highway extension.4

The Mackenzie Valley Highway — an 800+ km route from Wrigley to Norman Wells (Phase 1) and to Inuvik (Phase 2) — received construction approval with work starting summer 2026 and a revised cost estimate exceeding $2 billion.5 The Taltson Hydro Expansion ($2 billion proposed, 60 MW) would double the NWT's hydro capacity and deliver clean power to 11 communities serving approximately 70% of residents.6 The Pine Point zinc-lead mine ($653 million) is under review.7 The project database tracks 188 NWT projects and 52 energy-sector projects.8

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate fell 3.0 percentage points to 10.8% in February 20261, the largest single-month decline among all provinces and territories. The rate remains the highest in Canada, reflecting the structural employment constraints of a territory with 25 communities accessible only by air or seasonal sealift. The project database tracks 57 Nunavut projects, with 10 employment-sensitive projects.2

The federal government announced a $32 billion Northern Defence and Infrastructure investment covering Nunavut, including new Forward Operating Locations in Iqaluit and Northern Operation Support Nodes in Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet.3 Federal military hubs were also announced for Resolute.3 The federal Build Communities Strong Fund ($51 billion national) includes Nunavut allocations.4

Housing remains a central development constraint. The territory's target is 3,000 new units by 2030 with a $2.6 billion investment.5 The Nunavut 750 Homes Initiative — a tri-party agreement between the Government of Canada ($250 million), Government of Nunavut ($230 million), and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated — is under construction, with Baker Lake receiving the first 10 modular homes built by Ottawa manufacturer Caivan.6 Baffinland Iron Mines completed Inuit consultation for the Steensby Component of the Mary River project, clearing the final requirement to advance into construction at an estimated $3 billion.7 The Back River Gold Project ($610 million) is under construction in western Nunavut.8 Agnico Eagle operates as one of Nunavut's largest employers with over 2,000 positions, and gross mineral production exceeds $2.3 billion annually.5
